# (PART) Testing by Simulation {-}

# Null Distributions {#null-distributions}

## How Far Is Far Enough?

In Chapter \@ref(t-statistic), the ten scores sat about one standard error from 49 (t = 0.95) and nearly four standard errors from 46 (t = 3.79). The second t-value feels more convincing, but how far is far enough?

To answer that, we need to know what t-values look like when there is **no** real difference: when the population mean really is equal to the comparison value. That is the **null hypothesis**, and the spread of t-values we get when it is true is the **null distribution**. We will build it the way we built the distribution of sample means in Chapter \@ref(standard-error): take lots of samples and keep a result from each.

<div class="summary-box">
sample -> group mean -> t-value -> repeat many times -> null distribution -> which values are rare?
</div>

<div class="note">
**What you need for this chapter**

Chapters \@ref(functions) to \@ref(t-statistic), up to the one-sample t-test. You do not need the rest of Part I.
</div>

## A World Where The Null Is True

In real research we never know whether the null hypothesis is true. In a simulation, we can make it true on purpose.

Take a made-up question: are people called Steve taller than average? Picture a world where they are not. In the figure below, everyone's height has a mean of 175 cm and an SD of 7 cm, and Steves have exactly the same distribution. The heights are made up, but realistic for adults.

```{r steve-world, fig.cap="Left: in this world, the heights of people called Steve (dashed) match everyone's heights (filled) exactly. Right: a random sample of 10 Steves from that world. The heights are made up but realistic.", fig.alt="Two panels with height in centimetres on the x-axis. On the left, a filled normal curve for everyone and a dashed curve for people called Steve lie exactly on top of each other, centred on a dotted line at 175. On the right, ten dots for a sample of Steves, with a dotted line at 175 and a solid orange line at the sample mean of 179, about 4 cm higher.", echo=FALSE}
set.seed(4)
steves <- tibble(
  height = rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7),
  y = 1:10,
  panel = "Our sample"
)

world <- tibble(height = seq(150, 200, by = 0.5)) %>%
  mutate(density = dnorm(height, mean = 175, sd = 7), panel = "The world")

mean_lines <- tibble(
  panel = c("The world", "Our sample", "Our sample"),
  height = c(175, 175, mean(steves$height)),
  line = c("average", "average", "sample mean")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = world, aes(x = height, y = density, fill = "Everyone"),
            alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = world, aes(x = height, y = density,
                              colour = "People called Steve"),
            linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = steves, aes(x = height, y = y),
             size = 3, colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_vline(data = mean_lines, aes(xintercept = height, linetype = line),
             colour = c("grey20", "grey20", "#D55E00"), linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(panel, levels = c("The world", "Our sample")),
             scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c("Everyone" = "#467AAC")) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("People called Steve" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(NULL, values = c("average" = "dotted",
                                         "sample mean" = "solid")) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend(order = 1),
    colour = guide_legend(order = 2),
    linetype = guide_legend(
      order = 3, override.aes = list(colour = c("grey20", "#D55E00"))
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Height (cm)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 12),
        panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"))
```

```{r steve-world-code, ref.label="steve-world", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

```{r steve-world-reset, include=FALSE}
# put the random numbers back where they were, so the rest of the chapter
# is not affected by the Steve example
set.seed(123)
```

In this world, Steves are exactly average. That is what the null hypothesis says: there is no difference between Steves and everyone else. But the 10 Steves in our sample have a mean height of `r round(mean(steves$height), 1)` cm, about `r round(mean(steves$height) - 175)` cm above average. Nothing makes Steves taller here. The gap comes purely from which 10 Steves happened to end up in the sample: sampling noise.

A one-sample t-test would compare our sample mean with 175. So the real question is: how big a gap can sampling noise produce on its own, when the null hypothesis is true?

This chapter answers that by simulating the Steve world directly. `rnorm()` draws random values from a normal population. Here it draws a new group of 10 Steves, with heights from a population with a mean of 175 cm and an SD of 7 cm, and we calculate their t-value against 175:

```{r one-null-sample}
null_sample <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)
null_sample

my_t_value(null_sample, comparison_value = 175)
```

Run that chunk a few times. The heights change every time, and so does the t-value, even though nothing is going on: Steves are exactly average. The heights are in centimetres. The t-value makes the same comparison, the sample mean against 175, but measures the gap in standard errors: a t-value of 2 means the group's mean height is two standard errors above 175.

1. Click **+1** a few times. Watch each group of Steves, its mean, and where that mean lands.
2. Click **+10**, then **+100**. Compare the spread of the group means with the spread of individual heights in the top panel.
3. Tick **Expected shape**, and compare **SD of the means** with **Formula SE**.

Here is the same thing in R, with `replicate()` as in Chapter \@ref(standard-error): 1000 groups of 10 Steves, keeping each group's mean height.

```{r null-means-seed, include=FALSE}
# a fixed seed, so the numbers quoted below stay the same from render to render
set.seed(10)
```

```{r null-means}
null_means <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)))

c(sd_of_means = my_sd(null_means), formula_se = 7 / sqrt(10))
```

The group means bunch up far more tightly than individual heights. Individual Steves spread with an SD of 7 cm, but the group means spread by only about `r round(my_sd(null_means), 1)` cm: the standard error from Chapter \@ref(standard-error), 7 / √10 = `r round(7 / sqrt(10), 2)` cm.

A few groups still land well away from 175, though: the tallest of the 1000 groups averaged `r round(max(null_means), 1)` cm and the shortest `r round(min(null_means), 1)` cm. Every one of them came from a world where Steves are exactly average.

## One Group, One t-Value

Group means are in centimetres. A t-value makes the same comparison, the group mean against 175, but measures the gap in standard errors. The widget below works out one group's t-value step by step.

<iframe class="demyst-widget" src="apps/t-steps/embed.html" width="100%" height="700" title="One group, one t-value interactive widget" style="border: 0;"></iframe>

1. Click **Sample** to draw a group of 10 Steves. Watch the mean, SD and standard error fill in.
2. Click **Calculate t** to finish the equation.
3. Click **Add t** to put the t-value in the histogram.
4. Repeat a few times. Most t-values land near 0, and now and then one lands further out.

## Your Turn: Write `my_null_t()`

Now do the same in R. Wrap the steps from the one-sample chunk above in a function, so we can repeat them easily. It needs three inputs: the sample size, and the mean and SD of the population.

1. draw a sample with `rnorm()`;
2. calculate its t-value with `my_t_value()`, using the population mean as the comparison value.

Using the population mean as the comparison value is what makes the null hypothesis true.

```{r my-null-t-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <-
  output <-
  return(output)
}

my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`sample_values` uses `rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)`, and `output` uses `my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-null-t-solution}
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <- rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  output <- my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)
  return(output)
}

my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
```
`r unhide()`

## Check It Against R

Because `my_null_t()` uses random numbers, every run gives a different answer. To check it, we can make R repeat the same random numbers with `set.seed()`. With the same seed, `my_null_t()` should give exactly the same t-value as R's own `t.test()` on the same random sample:

```{r my-null-t-check}
set.seed(1)
mine <- my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)

set.seed(1)
r_version <- unname(
  t.test(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7), mu = 175)$statistic
)

c(mine = mine, R = r_version)
all.equal(mine, r_version)
```

## Many t-Values

Now repeat it 1000 times with `replicate()`:

```{r null-ts}
null_ts <- replicate(1000, my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7))
```

```{r null-histogram, fig.cap="1000 t-values from groups of 10 Steves in a world where the null hypothesis is true.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 simulated t-values centred on zero, with most between -2 and 2 and a few further out in both tails.", echo=FALSE}
ggplot(tibble(t = null_ts), aes(x = t)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, colour = "white", fill = "#467AAC") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r null-histogram-code, ref.label="null-histogram", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

This is the null distribution of t for samples of 10. Each t-value is one group of 10 Steves, compared with 175 and measured in standard errors instead of centimetres. Notice its shape:

- it is centred on 0, because on average the sample mean is right on the population mean;
- most t-values are between about -2 and 2;
- a few land further out, in both directions, even though the null is true.

Measuring in standard errors has a useful side effect. The null distribution of t has the same shape whatever the mean and SD of the population, as long as the sample size is the same: groups of 10 Steves, or of any other 10 values, give the same null distribution. The next chapter relies on that.

Which t-values are common, and which are rare? The widget below builds 1000 null t-values at a time. The slider picks out the rarest share of them, split between the two tails, so you can ask: how rare is this range of values?

<iframe class="demyst-widget" src="apps/rareness/embed.html" width="100%" height="480" title="Which t-values are rare interactive widget" style="border: 0;"></iframe>

1. Click **Regenerate** a few times. The details change every time, but the shape stays the same.
2. Move the slider. The orange values are the rarest ones, and the sentence under the plot says where they start.
3. How far from 0 do you have to go before only the rarest 5% are left? Is it the same after you regenerate?

## Where Do The Rare Values Start?

To find where the rarest values start in our own `null_ts`, put the t-values in order. `sort()` arranges a set of values from smallest to largest. `head()` shows the first six values and `tail()` the last six:

```{r sorted-ts}
sorted_ts <- sort(null_ts)

head(sorted_ts)
tail(sorted_ts)
```

Say we want to mark the rarest 5% of our 1000 t-values. 5% of 1000 is 50, so 25 in each tail:

- the **lower cutoff** is the 26th smallest t-value, so 25 values are below it;
- the **upper cutoff** is the 975th, so 25 values are above it (1000 - 975 = 25).

Square brackets pick out a value by its position: `sorted_ts[1]` is the smallest t-value and `sorted_ts[1000]` is the largest.

### Your Turn: Pick Them Out By Position

Use square brackets to pick the two cutoffs out of `sorted_ts`:

```{r cutoffs-by-position-exercise, eval=FALSE}
lower <-
upper <-

c(lower = lower, upper = upper)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
Put the position inside the square brackets: `sorted_ts[26]` for `lower`. Which position holds `upper`?
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r cutoffs-by-position-solution}
lower <- sorted_ts[26]
upper <- sorted_ts[975]

c(lower = lower, upper = upper)
```
`r unhide()`

### Your Turn: Write `my_cutoffs()`

The positions 26 and 975 only work for 1000 t-values and the rarest 5%. A function can work them out for any number of t-values and any share. Its second input, `alpha`, is the share of values we're marking as rare: `alpha = 0.05` marks the rarest 5%. The next chapter explains alpha properly.

1. sort the t-values;
2. count them with `length()`;
3. work out `k`, the number of values in each tail;
4. the lower cutoff is in position `k + 1`, and the upper cutoff is in position `n - k`.

```{r my-cutoffs-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <-
  n <-
  k <-
  lower <-
  upper <-
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs(null_ts)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`sorted` is `sort(null_ts)` and `n` is `length(sorted)`.

`k` is `floor(n * alpha / 2)`. With 1000 values, `1000 * 0.05 / 2` is 25. `floor()` rounds down to a whole number, because a position has to be a whole number: with 990 values, `990 * 0.05 / 2` is 24.75, and `floor()` makes it 24.

`lower` is `sorted[k + 1]` and `upper` is `sorted[n - k]`. With 1000 values, those are positions 26 and 975, the same as before.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-cutoffs-solution}
my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <- sort(null_ts)
  n <- length(sorted)
  k <- floor(n * alpha / 2)
  lower <- sorted[k + 1]
  upper <- sorted[n - k]
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs(null_ts)
```
`r unhide()`

You should get the same two values you picked out by position. Notice the default, `alpha = 0.05`, just like the defaults in Chapter \@ref(functions).

### See The Rare Values

Here is a plotting script to try different shares. Set `alpha_choice` to 0.5, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01, and run it each time. The orange bars are the t-values beyond the cutoffs, the dashed lines are the cutoffs, and the table counts the orange values. `|` means "or", so `rare` is `TRUE` for a t-value below the lower cutoff or above the upper one.

```{r rare-plot, fig.cap="The null t-values, with the rarest 5% (alpha_choice = 0.05) in orange and dashed lines at the cutoffs.", fig.alt="Histogram of 1000 null t-values in blue, with the bars beyond about -2.1 and 2.2 coloured orange and dashed vertical lines at those two values."}
alpha_choice <- 0.05
rare_cutoffs <- my_cutoffs(null_ts, alpha = alpha_choice)

null_t_data <- tibble(t = null_ts) %>%
  mutate(rare = t < rare_cutoffs[1] | t > rare_cutoffs[2])

ggplot(null_t_data, aes(x = t, fill = rare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_cutoffs, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#467AAC", "TRUE" = "#D55E00"),
                    guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

null_t_data %>%
  summarise(beyond = sum(rare), share = mean(rare))
```

With `alpha_choice = 0.05`, exactly `r sum(null_t_data$rare)` of the 1000 t-values are beyond the cutoffs, 25 in each tail: that is how we chose them. As the share gets smaller, the cutoffs move outwards, and only t-values further from 0 count as rare.

### Compare With R

R's `qt()` gives the cutoffs for the exact t distribution, which for samples of 10 has 9 degrees of freedom:

```{r cutoffs-compare}
tibble(
  cutoff = c("lower", "upper"),
  simulated = my_cutoffs(null_ts),
  qt = qt(c(0.025, 0.975), df = 9)
)
```

They are close, but not identical. Your cutoffs come from 1000 random samples, so they wobble a little every time you build a new `null_ts`, just like a sample mean wobbles around the population mean.

## Rare, But Not Impossible

Back to the groups of Steves. If Steves really are average, groups of 10 that come out particularly tall or short are rare. Of the 1000 group means in `null_means`, only `r sum(null_means > 180)` averaged more than 180 cm, and only `r sum(null_means < 170)` averaged less than 170 cm. The tallest 25 groups, the top 2.5%, all averaged more than `r round(sort(null_means)[975], 1)` cm.

Groups like those are rare enough that, if we ran the study once and got one of them, we might start to wonder whether something is going on with Steves. But there is no believable reason for Steves to be taller than anyone else. So even if our one group came out unusually tall, a fluke is still the better explanation.

Now picture a different study: people who were exposed to a certain toxin while they were growing up, compared with the average height. Suppose that group comes out unusually short. The result is exactly as rare as an unusually short group of Steves would be. What differs is the alternative. A toxin that affects growth is believable, so "something is going on" becomes a better explanation than a fluke.

There is a catch too. With the rarest 5% marked, 5% of null t-values land past the cutoffs. Check 100 different first names that are all truly average, and about 5 of them will look unusually tall or short from noise alone.

```{r my-functions-after-2a-null-distributions, eval=FALSE}
# Null Distributions -------------------------------------------------------
my_null_t <- function(n, pop_mean, pop_sd) {
  sample_values <- rnorm(n = n, mean = pop_mean, sd = pop_sd)
  output <- my_t_value(sample_values, comparison_value = pop_mean)
  return(output)
}

my_cutoffs <- function(null_ts, alpha = 0.05) {
  sorted <- sort(null_ts)
  n <- length(sorted)
  k <- floor(n * alpha / 2)
  lower <- sorted[k + 1]
  upper <- sorted[n - k]
  output <- c(lower, upper)
  return(output)
}
```
The rest of your file depends on which chapters you have done so far.

Then check that the saved file works on its own. This is the last chunk of the exercise file:

```{r toolbox-saved-check, eval=FALSE}
rm(list = ls())
source("my_functions.R")

set.seed(1)
mine <- my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
set.seed(1)
r_version <- unname(
  t.test(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7), mu = 175)$statistic
)
all.equal(mine, r_version)

# 20:1 counts down from 20 to 1; with alpha = 0.1, one value is in each tail
all.equal(my_cutoffs(20:1, alpha = 0.1), c(2, 19))
```

You should see two `TRUE`s:

```text

[1] TRUE
```
